610.title: Correct, or be kind
610.hook: if you can, correct them; if not, kindness was given you for this (Meditations 9.11)
610.howItsDone: People who draw on this entry often decide deliberately whether a correction can actually be heard; when it can't, they choose a concrete kindness instead of repeating the point.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was three presents: judgment, action, acceptance, all here now. Your line was it suffices.

A friend says something you're fairly sure is wrong. Not dangerous, just wrong: a bad plan, a mistaken idea about a coworker, a choice about their kids. You can feel the correction loading in your mouth. And then a second voice: is this the moment? Will they hear it? Marcus met that fork too. In book nine he wrote down what to do when correcting doesn't work.
screen: `THE CORRECTION LOADING.` → `IS THIS THE MOMENT?` → `CORRECT, OR BE KIND.`

segments.voice: If you can, Marcus writes, set them right by teaching. Correction isn't forbidden; a friend who never tells you the truth isn't much of a friend. But if you can't, remember that kindness was given to you for exactly this. Not as decoration, not as a personality trait, but as equipment for the moment correction fails. Then the surprising part. Even the gods, Marcus says, are kind to such people. They help them to health, to wealth, to reputation; that's how generous they are. Whatever you believe about the gods, look at the logic. If the highest powers keep helping people who get things wrong, then kindness can't be a prize for being right. It's given to the wrong as well. And the last line: it's in your power too, he says. Or tell me: who's stopping you? His point: no circumstance can take away the ability to be kind. The other person can refuse your correction. Your kindness is yours to give, whether they take it well or not. It's a close cousin of the third door, from book eight. Here the second door gets a warmer name. Not bear: be kind.

segments.voice: Think of one person you've wanted to correct lately, and ask honestly: could they hear it, and is it yours to give? 611.title: Not Plato's Republic
611.hook: don't hope for a perfect world; be content if the smallest thing goes forward (Meditations 9.29)
611.howItsDone: People who take this line seriously tend to set small, concrete goals inside big problems, and count each small step as real progress rather than waiting for a complete solution.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was correct: teach if you can, and if not, be kind. Your line was who's stopping you.

The town meeting runs all evening and ends with a vote to study the issue further. The group project has one person doing all the work. The world's problems are so big you can't even find the edge of one to hold on to. It's easy to decide that nothing you do matters unless it fixes everything. Marcus ran an empire, and in book nine he answered that pull with a five-word line.
screen: `ALL EVENING, NO DECISION.` → `IT MATTERS ONLY IF IT FIXES ALL?` → `NOT PLATO'S REPUBLIC.`

segments.voice: He begins: the cause of all things is like a rushing river; it carries everything along. And how cheap, he says, are the little men who play at statesmanship and imagine they're doing philosophy. Then the line, in George Long's 1862 translation: “Do not expect Plato's Republic.” Plato wrote a whole dialogue imagining the perfect city, ruled by philosophers. Marcus, a ruler who wrote philosophy, tells himself not to expect it. Instead, be content if the smallest thing goes forward, and don't think that outcome is a small matter. Why? Who, he asks, can change people's beliefs? And without a change of belief, what do you get but people groaning while they pretend to obey? Force can make a law. It can't make a heart agree. Marcus mentions rulers, Alexander and Philip among them, and says if they only played the tragic hero, no one has sentenced him to copy them. The work of philosophy, he writes, is simple and modest; don't lead me into pomposity. He also tells himself to do what nature asks right now, without looking around to see whether anyone will know. So the hope isn't the perfect city. It's the next small thing, moved forward one honest inch.

segments.voice: Pick one problem that feels too big, in your work, your family, your town, the world, and for one breath let it be too big. Then look for the smallest thing in it that could go forward this week: one email, one conversation, one bag of litter, one hour of help. Make it small enough that you could actually do it, and see yourself doing it.

612.title: Pray differently
612.hook: pray not "let me get this" but "let me not crave it," not "let me be rid of it" but "let me not fear" (Meditations 9.40)
612.howItsDone: Readers who take up this entry often notice the fear or craving beneath a hope, and those who pray sometimes ask for steadiness alongside the outcome they want, in the words of their own tradition.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was rushing river, and Marcus asking only that the smallest thing move forward. Your line was the smallest thing.

Late at night, the asking comes. Let the test come back clear. Let me get the job. Let this pain go away. Let my kid be okay. People of every faith, and people of none, find themselves sending wishes like these out into the dark. Marcus did too. Near the end of book nine he wrote a short reflection on his own prayers, and it turns the asking around.
screen: `LATE AT NIGHT, THE ASKING.` → `LET THIS PASS.` → `PRAY DIFFERENTLY.`

segments.voice: Either the gods have power or they don't, Marcus writes. If they don't, why pray at all? If they do, why not pray for the power not to fear these things, not to crave them, not to grieve over them, rather than praying only that they come or don't come? Someone might say: the gods put that in my own power. Then, Marcus answers, isn't it better to use what's in your power with freedom than to strain like a slave after what isn't? And who told you the gods don't help us even with what's in our power? Then his examples. One person prays: how can I win that woman? You: how can I stop wanting to? Another: how can I be rid of this? You: how can I stop needing to be rid of it? Another: how can I not lose my little son? You: how can I not be afraid to lose him? Turn your prayers this way, he says, and see what comes. Read him fairly. Marcus is writing to himself, a Stoic, about his own prayers, not anyone else's. People in many traditions pray for healing and for their children, and many also pray for courage and peace in the same breath. And the little son is not abstract. Marcus and his wife Faustina lost a number of their children young.

613.title: Will you ever be good?
613.hook: will you ever be simple, whole, unconcealed? (Meditations 10.1)
613.howItsDone: Readers of the Meditations sometimes use Marcus's opening question in book ten as an honest self-check, asking where they present a different self in different rooms, and choosing one place to be plainer.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was pray differently: not only let this pass, but let me not fear it. Your line was let me not fear.

A face for work. A face for family dinners. A face for the group chat. Each one fits, and each can be a little tiring to wear. Underneath them all, someone is doing the switching. Book ten of the Meditations opens with Marcus asking about that someone, not as a theory, but in the second person, like someone gently shaking his own shoulder.
screen: `A FACE FOR EVERY ROOM.` → `WHO'S UNDERNEATH?` → `BOOK TEN OPENS.`

segments.voice: Marcus speaks to his own soul: will you ever, my soul, be good and simple and one and naked, plainer to see than the body that surrounds you? It isn't a rule. It's a question he doesn't know the answer to. Take the words. Good. Simple: single, one fold, not doubled over. One: whole, not split into different pieces for different rooms. Naked: unconcealed, nothing hidden under the surface that would contradict what shows. And the questions keep coming. Will you ever, he asks, taste a loving and contented disposition? Be full, needing nothing, craving nothing, not wanting more time to enjoy pleasures, or a better place, or nicer weather, or better company? Will you be satisfied with what's here, and believe that all is well with you? Why this matters on a Tuesday: some tiredness may not come from the work at all, but from the switching, minding the gap between the person inside and the one we're presenting. Marcus wants to close that gap. Not by telling everyone everything; simple doesn't mean blurting. It means there's one person in there, the same in every room. And notice how he asks: as a question, to himself, with no answer written down.

segments.voice: Think of a room in your life where you wear the heaviest face: a meeting, a family visit, a feed. Choose one small, true thing you could let show, a real opinion kindly said, a real feeling, a plain no, and breathe with it.

614.title: Formed to bear it
614.hook: whatever happens, you're either made to bear it or not; if not, it will end (Meditations 10.3)
614.howItsDone: Stoic readers often separate a hardship into the event itself and the judgments added to it, and work on the judgments, while still seeking practical and medical help where it's needed.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was contented disposition, and Marcus asking his soul to be simple and whole. Your line was simple and whole.

A long night in a hospital waiting room. A hard season at work. A grief that isn't going anywhere fast. Someone tells you, you're stronger than you think. Sometimes that helps. Sometimes it feels like being handed a heavier box. Marcus has his own version of that sentence in book ten of the Meditations, but his is stranger, and in an odd way more honest, because it has two halves.
screen: `A LONG NIGHT IN A WAITING ROOM.` → `STRONGER THAN YOU THINK?` → `FORMED TO BEAR IT.`

segments.voice: Everything that happens, Marcus writes, happens either in a way you're formed by nature to bear, or in a way you're not. If it's the kind you're formed to bear, don't complain. Bear it, as you were made to. If it's the kind you're not formed to bear, don't complain either, because it will come to an end, once it has used you up. That's blunt, and it's meant to be honest. For Marcus, nothing truly unbearable goes on forever; it has an end built into it. Then he adds a further sentence: remember that you're formed to bear everything that your own judgment can make bearable, by thinking of it as in your interest, or as your duty. In other words, a great deal of what feels impossible is made heavier by the story we tell about it. Change the story, and the weight can change. That isn't a promise for every pain. Some pain is in the body, some is grief, and no story removes it. Nothing in this passage says you have to carry anything alone, either; asking for help is also a way of bearing. But Marcus's question is worth keeping: which part of this weight is the thing itself, and which part is what I've told myself about it?

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing you've been carrying, a moderate weight, not the heaviest, and look at it in two parts: the thing itself, and the story on top of it, it's not fair, it'll never change, I can't. Breathe, and see whether one piece of the story could be set down. Then ask whether you can bear this today; if not, remember it won't last forever, and that you can ask for help. If a weight ever feels like too much, please reach out: in the US, call or text 988, or call local emergency help.

615.title: Keep the names
615.hook: good, modest, truthful, even-minded: keep these names and deserve them (Meditations 10.8)
615.howItsDone: Some readers of the Meditations choose one of Marcus's names each morning, truthful or even-minded, say, and return to it during the day whenever they notice they've let it slip.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was fork, and the question of which part of a weight is the story. Your line was made to bear it.

A name tag at a conference. A title in an email signature. Mom, coach, nurse, friend. Names do work: they tell people what to expect from us, and they quietly tell us what to expect from ourselves. In book ten Marcus picks out a short list of names he wants to answer to, and then he tells himself something harder. Don't just wear them. Deserve them.
screen: `A NAME TAG.` → `NAMES DO WORK.` → `KEEP THE NAMES.`

segments.voice: Once you've taken these names, Marcus writes, good, modest, truthful, rational, even-minded, high-minded, take care not to trade them for others. And if you lose them, come back to them quickly. He defines three of them. Rational means paying attention: looking at each thing carefully, not carelessly. Even-minded means accepting willingly what the nature of the whole hands you. High-minded means lifting your mind above the body's pleasures and pains, above shabby fame, and above death. Hold on to the names, he says, without wanting other people to call you by them. A name you live by is different from a name you're given. The coach who's called coach but never shows up has the name and not the thing. Then a hard picture. Going on as before, torn and stained, Marcus says, is like the fighters in the arena, half eaten by wild beasts, covered in wounds and blood, still begging to be kept until tomorrow, only to be thrown again to the same claws. It's a brutal image, and he turns it on himself: fix yourself in these few names, he says, and stay in them. And if you feel yourself slipping, go off bravely to some quiet corner where you can hold on to them again.

616.title: Get to know change
616.hook: study how all things change into one another (Meditations 10.11)
616.howItsDone: Some Stoic readers practice contemplating change, watching a flame, a season or their own body, as a way to hold things more lightly and to stay focused on acting justly now.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was arena, and Marcus's six names to keep. Your line was keep the name.

Take one photo of the same tree every week for a year, and the strip of pictures tells a story no single photo can. Buds, leaves, gold, bare branches, snow. It never stops changing; we just don't look closely enough to see it happen. In book ten Marcus treats watching change closely as a discipline of its own, a part of philosophy to train in.
screen: `ONE TREE, EVERY WEEK.` → `IT NEVER STOPS.` → `GET TO KNOW CHANGE.`

segments.voice: Learn the way of looking that sees how all things change into one another, Marcus writes. Keep attending to it, and train yourself in this part of philosophy. Nothing, he says, is so fitted to produce greatness of mind. Someone who really sees that everything is changing loosens their grip. They stop clutching, because there's nothing to clutch that will hold still. That person, he says, has in a way already set the body aside, knowing they must leave the human world, no one knows how soon. They give themselves wholly to justice in what they do, and to the nature of the whole in everything else. What others say or think or do against them doesn't occupy them. Two things are enough for them: to act justly now, and to be content with what is given now. And the week, looking back: correct or be kind, the smallest thing, let me not fear, simple and whole, made to bear it, keep the name, and now, study change. Under all seven lies the same ground: things are moving. People change, troubles end, prayers turn, names slip and come back. Watch change closely, and you hold everything a little more lightly, and act a little more justly. Marcus calls that greatness of mind, and he thinks you build it by looking.

Marcus, who trained himself to watch how all things change into one another, calling it a discipline that builds greatness of mind. Today's word.
